name: Web49 (miniwasm interpreter)
baseline: wasm3 (the fastest WebAssembly interpreter incumbent; wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR and V8 are not in the published charts)
workload: Wall-clock time of C benchmarks compiled with emcc -O2 and run once each by wasm3 and by miniwasm: binary-trees 16, coremark 3000, fannkuch-redux 10, fib_i32 40, mandelbrot 2000 (plain and SIMD), nbody 2000000, and a trap-execution test.
claimed_speedup: Bar charts only, no numeric table. Values read off the chart images by eye (approximate): fib_i32 40 about 3.0 s (wasm3) vs 1.17 s (miniwasm), roughly 2.6x (derived from page data); binary-trees 16 about 3.0 s vs 1.95 s (1.5x); fannkuch-redux 10 about 1.63 s vs 1.15 s (1.4x); nbody about 1.95 s vs 1.57 s (1.25x); mandelbrot 2000 about 1.46 s vs 1.30 s (1.1x); mandelbrot-simd about 1.06 s vs 0.91 s (1.2x); coremark 3000 about 3.4 s vs 3.2 s (1.06x). Trap test is slower: about 0.0055 s (wasm3) vs 0.027 s (miniwasm), roughly 5x worse.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark wasm modules built with emcc -O2 (bench.py default, no extra emcc flags). Engine built with make CC=gcc ('gcc is fastest in my tests' per README); the exact optimisation flags of the miniwasm and wasm3 builds, and the wasm3 version, are not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded interpreter; wasm text format about 95%, binary format about 100%, spec tests about 75% complete per README (v0.0.1 first release). Bundles a custom WASI implementation and a small wat2wasm/wasm2wat/wasm2wasm toolkit that is much smaller than WABT or Binaryen. Uses threaded-code dispatch and basic-block versioning from the author's MiniVM; the README says computed-goto style macros (NEXT, LABEL) would need rewriting for MSVC.
caveats: Numbers exist only as PNG bar charts, each benchmark was run once by default (bench.py runs=1; trap and nop use more), on one M1 laptop with no CPU frequency or noise control. Margins on coremark and mandelbrot are within what laptop run-to-run noise can produce; only fib_i32, binary-trees and fannkuch-redux show clear gaps. Startup/trap handling is about 5x slower than wasm3. bench.py also lists wasmer and wasmtime as extra engines, but the published charts show only wasm3 and miniwasm, so no claim against wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR or V8 is verified. The Hacker News thread was not readable here (HN blocked); the search snippet says the author found WABT's interpreter too slow and wasm3 faster but interpreter-only. Chart values are my visual readings, not page text.
found_via: Hacker News via WebSearch (site news.ycombinator.com): 'Show HN: I wrote a WebAssembly Interpreter and Toolkit in C' (item 34310395); snippet linked the project at github.com/fastvm. HN thread itself not opened (blocked).
